title: Nadar: the kindly glance
hookLine: effort matters, but the Granth speaks of grace, the Beloved's glance, as what finally opens the door

cards: A school play. A nervous kid in the back row has rehearsed for weeks, knows every line, and still freezes when the lights come up. Then they catch a parent's eye in the audience, and the parent gives the smallest nod.
That's all. And the kid breathes, and speaks. All the practice mattered.
But it was the glance that opened the door.

teach.b: Today's word is nadar. It comes from the Persian nazar: sight, a look, a glance. In the Granth it means the Beloved's kindly glance: grace, given, not earned.
Once you know the word, you'll find it everywhere. The Mool Mantar ends with gur prasaad: by the Guru's grace.
Pauri 4 of the Japji puts it in one line: karmee aavai kaparraa, nadaree mokh duaar. By your deeds comes this garment, this life, this body.
By the glance of grace comes the door of liberation. Pauri 32, where you climbed the ladder of the Name, ended: Nanak nadaree paaeeai, by grace it's reached.

And the last pauri, the goldsmith's shop, closed with nadaree nadar nihaal: with a glance, the Gracious One fills them with joy. So the Granth holds two things together, and it's worth being careful here. Effort matters.
The Gurus worked, served, sang, and taught others to live honestly and remember the Name. The ladder is real, and you climb it. But climbing isn't the same as arriving.
The glance isn't a reward you can demand, like a paycheck.
It's more like the nod from the audience, from someone who has been watching with love all along. In the Granth's picture, you do your part, and the door is not yours to force.

how: Sikhs recite gur prasaad, by the Guru's grace, as the last words of the Mool Mantar, and many speak of any good outcome as coming through the Guru's kirpa, grace, while still working hard for it.

o: the evil eye, a jealous look
a reward earned by good deeds

games.q: what's inside nadar — tap the pairs.
p: by grace, the door of liberation

s: in the Granth, grace makes effort unnecessary
effort matters; the Granth holds the climbing and the glance together.
nadar comes from the Persian nazar, a look or glance
a glance of grace, given not earned.
the Mool Mantar ends with gur prasaad, by the Guru's grace
grace is there from the very first lines.

games.q: you've climbed the ladder, step by step, for years. in Japji 4, what finally opens the door?
games.why: karmee aavai kaparraa, nadaree mokh duaar: by deeds comes this life; by grace, the door of liberation.

practice: Think of one good thing in your life you didn't earn: a person who loves you, your health today, a chance someone gave you before you deserved it. Let yourself feel thankful, not for your own effort but for the gift.
If you pray, thank the One for it silently, in your own way; if not, let the thanks sit warm in your chest, and breathe with it.

wordCard.voice: Nadar. The kindly glance: grace, given, not earned. Effort climbs the ladder, and in the Granth, the glance is what opens the door.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: nadar, the kindly glance; grace, from Persian nazar.

carryVoice: Your line: the glance comes. You do your part; the door opens by grace. A full week, closed with a glance.
